passage:
In the corner of his room in a Lajpat Nagar flat, Ojas had his chemistry book open at the mole concept, earphones in, a Punjabi playlist singing loudly in his ears. His phone lay beside the book, buzzing every few seconds with the class group arguing about a cricket match.
He read the definition of a mole. Buzz. He replied with a laughing face. Read it again. A chorus in his ear made him hum along. By ten o'clock he had read the same page six times and could not have explained a single line.
Next morning, in the unit test, the question on moles looked completely new. Trisha, beside him, was writing steadily. She had revised in the silent reading room downstairs, phone in her bag.

qa.q: How many times had Ojas read the same page by ten o'clock?
qa.a: He had read the same page six times.

qa.q: Why did the mole question look completely new to Ojas?
qa.a: His attention kept being pulled away by the buzzing phone and the lyrics, so nothing from the page settled into memory, even though he felt he had studied.

qa.q: What could Ojas change the next time he revises?
qa.a: Put the phone in another room, switch to silence or music without words, and study in short focused blocks, maybe in the reading room like Trisha.

qa.q: How might Trisha see the difference between their evenings?
qa.a: Trisha probably realises her quiet hour with the phone put away gave her more than Ojas got from a long, noisy evening.

grounding: It shows a teenager studying with a buzzing phone and lyrics in his ears whose chemistry doesn't stick because his attention is overloaded.

passage:
"Vasu, are you studying or partying?" Parul didi stood in the doorway.
"Studying! History." Vasudha pulled out one earbud. A song was blasting.
"With that playing? And your phone's lit up like a festival."
"I focus better with music. And I have to reply, it's the group project chat."
"Okay. Tell me three causes of the revolt of 1857."
Vasudha opened her mouth. "Umm... the cartridges. And... wait, I just read this."
"How long have you been reading?"
"An hour."
"And you remember the cartridges." Parul sat on the bed. "Try twenty minutes. Phone in my room. Music without words, if you want. Then I'll ask again."
Vasudha groaned, but handed over the phone.
Twenty minutes later she rattled off four causes without stopping.

qa.q: How long had Vasudha been reading?
qa.a: Vasudha had been reading for an hour.

qa.q: What does Vasudha's "wait, I just read this" reveal about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt surprised and a little embarrassed 😅; she believed she had been studying, but with the song and the chat pulling at her attention, the causes hadn't stuck.

qa.q: Why did Parul's twenty-minute test work?
qa.a: It removed the phone and the lyrics for one short, clear block, so Vasudha's attention could stay on the material, and the quick check showed the difference.

qa.q: How does Parul didi see Vasudha's way of studying?
qa.a: Parul sees it as closer to partying than studying, and cares enough to prove it gently with a test instead of a lecture.

grounding: It shows a teenager studying with lyrics and a busy chat whose history doesn't stick until the distractions are removed.

passage:
I'm Santosh. In Class 11 I had a habit I was proud of: I could study, chat and listen to rap all at the same time. I'd tell Hansa, "Multitasking, yaar." Hansa just shook her head.
Then came the physics half-yearly. I had spent whole evenings "revising" circular motion, but in the exam the formulas were mush. I knew I had seen them. I just couldn't find them.
Hansa had studied fewer hours than me and scored way higher. She told me she put her phone in a drawer and kept things quiet for fifty minutes at a stretch.
I tried it the next month, grumbling. No lyrics, no pings. It was boring at first. But in the next test the formulas were just there, as if they had been waiting for me.

qa.q: Which topic had Santosh been revising before the half-yearly?
qa.a: Santosh had been revising circular motion.

qa.q: Why was Santosh proud of studying, chatting and listening to rap together?
qa.a: It felt efficient and clever, like getting more done, so Santosh didn't notice the overload was stopping the formulas from sticking.

qa.q: What worked for Hansa, and could it work for others?
qa.a: Putting the phone in a drawer and keeping things quiet for fifty minutes at a stretch; it gives attention one job, which helps memory for most people.

qa.q: What might Hansa have thought when Santosh said "Multitasking"?
qa.a: Hansa probably thought it wasn't working but didn't want to argue, which is why the only answer was a shake of the head.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose physics revision didn't stick while studying with chat and lyrics, because attention and memory were overloaded.

passage:
Tutor's note, Wednesday evening batch. Jeevan
Anirban (Class 10) sat through the whole revision hour on circle theorems with one earbud in, film songs leaking out, and his phone face up, lighting every few seconds with group messages. He nodded along and copied everything neatly. At the end I gave a five-question check. He got one right and said, "But I understood it while you were teaching, sir!" He looked genuinely confused.
What I did next: I asked him to try Friday's hour with the phone in my drawer and no music, just as an experiment. On Friday he fidgeted for ten minutes, then settled. He scored four out of five on a similar check and grinned. I've suggested he try the same at home and tell me how it goes.

qa.q: How many questions did Anirban get right on Wednesday's check?
qa.a: He got one right.

qa.q: Why was Anirban genuinely confused by his score?
qa.a: He felt he had understood while copying and nodding, not noticing that the songs and buzzing messages kept the ideas from sticking.

qa.q: What experiment did Jeevan suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Keeping the phone in the drawer and the music off for one hour; with fewer things pulling at his attention, the theorems stuck and he scored four.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jeevan to see Anirban grin on Friday?
qa.a: Jeevan would likely feel pleased and hopeful, having helped a student find this out through his own experiment instead of a scolding.

grounding: A tutor notes a teenager whose learning does not stick while music and a buzzing phone overload his attention, and how removing them helps.

passage:
Tuesday, 10:30 pm
Three hours on biology tonight. Photosynthesis. I had my playlist on, the one with the loud Tamil songs, and the class group was going crazy about the cricket match, so my phone buzzed every minute. I kept replying "lol" and reading the same paragraph about chlorophyll.
Just now Lalit called to quiz me for tomorrow's test. He asked, "What are the two stages?" Blank. Totally blank. I could remember every line of the song, though. Every line!
Lalit said, "Your brain is doing three jobs at once." Annoying, but maybe true.
Tomorrow morning: one hour, phone in Amma's room, no songs. Let's see.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What question did Lalit ask?
qa.a: "What are the two stages?"

qa.q: What does Chaitanya remembering every line of the song suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Chaitanya's attention was going to the music and messages rather than the biology, which is frustrating after three hours of trying 😅

qa.q: What plan does Chaitanya make, and why might it work?
qa.a: One hour in the morning with the phone in Amma's room and no songs; with fewer demands on attention, the biology has a better chance to stick.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel quizzing a friend who draws a blank?
qa.a: Lalit may be surprised and a little worried about the test, and cares enough to point out the problem even if it annoys.

grounding: A teenager studies for hours with loud songs and a buzzing phone and finds the biology did not stick.
